newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-U.S. crew circle Mir in escape capsule.
newsitem.headline: Russian-U.S. crew circle Mir in escape capsule.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts and a U.S. astronaut spent about 45 minutes circling the crippled Mir space station in their Soyuz escape capsule on Friday as part of preparations for risky repair work.

Mission Control officials said commander Anatoly Solovyov guided the Soyuz manually back to Mir after he, engineer Pavel Vinogradov and British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale filmed the station, damaged in an accident on June 25.
"We've touched gently," Solovyov said in a radio link-up with Mission Control at Korolyov just outside Moscow.
The three-man crew were expected to remain in the escape capsule for about an hour before entering Mir.
Film footage from the Soyuz, fed directly to Mission Control, showed the craft moving slowly away from Mir and then approaching it as it redocked at 6:13 p.m. (1413 GMT).
The new crew is preparing to fix damage done when Mir collided with its cargo ship while it was redocking in June. The accident was the worst mishap in Mir's 11 years in orbit.
The Soyuz undocked on one side of Mir on Friday and redocked on the opposite side near the Spektr module which was punctured during the June collision.
Redocking near the Spektr means the cosmonauts will be able to make a quick escape if anything goes wrong during the repairs, which will include sealing the Spektr.

Previous commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin returned safely to earth on Thursday after enduring one of the most gruelling six months in the history of human space flight.
The new crew enjoyed a change of luck on Thursday when they repaired the main Elektron oxygen generating system just as the old crew shut the hatch on their Soyuz capsule, officials said.
Flight officials were relieved that the oxygen system was repaired, eliminating concern that they might have to wait for the U.S. shuttle to bring new parts in late September.
But the prospect of the undocking and redocking caused a few jitters at Mission Control.
"An undocking is a pretty tense event," said Yuri Antoshechkin, head of Mission Control's analysis team.

The Spektr module now is sealed off from the rest of the station. The two Russian cosmonauts will open the hatch next Wednesday to reattach cables linked to Spektr's solar panels to restore the ship's energy system.

To prepare for the Friday Soyuz trip, the crew shut off the oxygen system they had worked so hard to repair. "We turned it on yesterday evening and it worked fine until this morning, and we have turned it off for two reasons," Antoshechkin said.

"One, to lower energy demands on the station during the undocking today," he said. "And second, because it can only be turned off by the crew, and in case that, knock on wood (for luck), the undocking fails, then we couldn't turn it off later."
All three crew members were packed into the Soyuz for Friday's flight because space officials do not want to leave anyone on Mir without an emergency escape vehicle.
On Sunday, Mir will redock with its old Progress resupply ship, the very procedure that caused the June accident. This time however the crew expects to do the operation on automatic pilot.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin were undergoing rehabilitation and readjustment to life with gravity on Friday at the Star City cosmonaut training centre outside Moscow, officials said.
Mishaps during their six-month mission include a fire, loss of station's orientation, an irregular heartbeat suffered by Tsibliyev and problems with the power and oxygen supplies.
